segments.title: The 1890s "real" pre-dreadnoughts
segments.body: The episode calls these ships the "real" pre-dreadnoughts and compares France's Charlemagne class with Sweden's Oden class. Charlemagne represents the large ocean-going battleship, while Oden belongs to the smaller coastal-defence tradition. The pairing frames the main problem: a navy defending home waters may need a different ship from one expected to project power at range. Their size, armament, and intended employment provide concrete ways to compare late-19th-century fleet doctrine and the risks each design imposed on an opponent.

evidence.note: After the Archer class, the series moves into the 1890s through Sweden's Oden class and France's Charlemagne class.

segments.summary: The episode sets French Charlemagne-class ships beside Sweden's Oden class to examine two sharply different answers to late-19th-century naval defence.

segments.title: Charlemagne's heavy but awkward design
segments.body: The Charlemagne class carried two twin 12-inch turrets, ten 5.5-inch guns, eight 3.9-inch guns, twenty 47 mm weapons, and four 450 mm torpedo tubes. Its flared hull is unmistakably French, while the overall design did not always work well. The armament looks formidable on paper, although balance and handling are separate questions. The secondary battery may have been light for a full pre-dreadnought, especially given the handling demands and tactical expectations of the period.

evidence.note: The Charlemagne class combined a flared hull with structural problems, 12-inch and secondary guns, lighter weapons, and torpedo tubes.

segments.summary: Charlemagne's flared hull, 12-inch guns, secondary battery, and torpedo tubes show both the firepower and the design compromises of an early French pre-dreadnought.

segments.title: French arsenals and uneven building speed
segments.body: The Charlemagne-class construction dates at the Brest and Lorient arsenals show how uneven French output could be. Charlemagne and Saint Louis moved slowly from laying down to completion, while Gaulois was laid down in January 1896, launched in October 1896, and commissioned in January 1899. The last ship started therefore entered service first. Gaulois shows that French yards could build rapidly when their priorities aligned, and all three ships carried Harvey armour. The comparison places the output problem in shipbuilding organisation and political choices rather than a lack of technical ability.

evidence.note: The laying-down, launch, and commissioning dates of Charlemagne, Saint Louis, and Gaulois reveal sharply uneven French arsenal productivity.

segments.summary: The completion dates of Charlemagne, Saint Louis, and Gaulois expose how French shipbuilding could be both slow to start and unexpectedly quick to finish.

segments.title: Oden class: compact coastal battle power
segments.body: The Oden class carried two 10-inch guns, six 4.7-inch guns, ten 57 mm weapons, and an 18-inch torpedo tube on only 3,445 tons. Charlemagne displaced 11,275 tons, more than three times as much. That comparison does not make Oden an equal in open-water fighting. It shows why an attacker could not dismiss the compact coastal battleship as a patrol craft or minor obstacle. A small coastal navy could force an opponent to bring heavier and more expensive ships than the defender's tonnage alone would suggest.

evidence.note: Oden concentrated a substantial armament on 3,445 tons, compared with the Charlemagne class's 11,275 tons.

segments.summary: Sweden's Oden class concentrates enough guns in a 3,445-ton coastal ship to make an attacker commit much larger and costlier vessels.

segments.title: Jeune École ideas with battleship hedging
segments.body: Both navies fit within a broad Jeune École and flotilla-defence tradition, where torpedo craft, cruisers, and defensive waters matter heavily. Sweden's Oden class belongs naturally in that system because it was designed for nearby waters and national defence. France, however, still built Charlemagne as a full battleship with 18 knots of speed and about 4,200 nautical miles of range at 10 knots. That endurance made the ship more than a harbour guard or coast-defence craft. Keeping battleships in the programme despite official enthusiasm for small-craft doctrine suggests caution about the theory's limits.

evidence.note: French and Swedish flotilla-defence approaches diverged because France continued building ocean-going battleships alongside its smaller craft.

segments.summary: France and Sweden both use flotilla-defence logic, but France keeps building ocean-going battleships as insurance against the limits of that theory.

segments.title: Oden's guns and the torpedo-boat problem
segments.body: Oden's 4.7-inch and 57 mm guns give it a credible answer to torpedo boats, which matters because small craft were central to late-19th-century coastal defence arguments. Its 10-inch guns still demand respect from larger attackers, but the calibre is awkward. A 10-inch gun has much of the loading, handling, and installation burden of a 12-inch weapon without matching its striking power. It also lacks the faster fire and easier handling of smaller heavy guns such as 9.2-inch or 8-inch weapons. Oden's 84.8 metre length, 14.78 metre beam, 5.28 metre draught, 3,445-ton displacement, and 16.5-knot speed make those compromises visible in the ship's whole design.

evidence.note: Oden's secondary battery could counter torpedo boats, while her 10-inch guns and compact dimensions embodied the trade-offs of a coastal battleship.

segments.summary: Oden's secondary battery gives it a real answer to torpedo boats, while its 10-inch guns reveal the compromises inside compact coastal battleship design.

segments.title: Coastal defence as force multiplication
segments.body: A coastal ship belonged inside a wider defensive system rather than a lone duel at sea. A ship like Oden could operate with forts and torpedo-boat flotillas, so an enemy could not assume that one battleship would solve the problem. The attacker might need to send multiple expensive capital ships merely to suppress or intimidate a few smaller defenders. This was the economic and strategic value of the coastal-defence ship: it could force an opponent to overcommit without being designed to win an oceanic battle-line engagement.

evidence.note: Small coastal battleships backed by forts and flotillas could force an attacker to commit a larger number of expensive capital ships.

segments.summary: Backed by forts and flotillas, several compact coastal ships can force an attacker to commit a much larger battle fleet simply to threaten the coast.

segments.title: A risk fleet must remain defensive
segments.body: Risk-fleet theory raises the question of whether navies ignored new strategic ideas or adapted them to their own circumstances. A true risk fleet would be powerful enough to make Britain reluctant to fight, yet too limited to make Britain feel compelled to eliminate it. Germany's battleships, battlecruisers, dreadnoughts, and colonial ambitions did not fit that narrow deterrent model because they gave the fleet real offensive reach. Britain then had a reason to answer it directly. Range, mission, and offensive capability shaped whether a rival saw the fleet as insurance or a threat.

evidence.note: The transcript defines a risk fleet and contrasts defensive deterrence with Germany's offensive naval capability.

segments.summary: The video distinguishes a defensive risk fleet, meant to deter Britain, from Germany's offensive battle fleet with colonial and long-range ambitions.

segments.title: A German fleet built for continental defence
segments.body: The episode explores a counterfactual in which Germany builds powerful but clearly local coastal-defence forces while leaving colonial work to cruisers. Such a force could still deter or fight France if its range and operational assumptions kept it focused on nearby waters. Britain might then have had less reason to treat it as a direct global challenge. Long-range cruisers could handle colonial work while the battle fleet remained short-ranged and focused on France. The scenario links naval range and mission to the Entente Cordiale and the road to the First World War.

evidence.note: The transcript considers German ships focused on France, cruiser support for colonies, and the possible British diplomatic response.

segments.summary: A short-range German battle fleet directed at France, backed by long-range cruisers, might have looked less threatening to Britain and altered diplomatic pressure.

segments.title: Coastal defence and Russia's road to Tsushima
segments.body: These coastal-defence ships and their successors are presented as a factor in Russia's subsequent naval buildup. That enlarged fleet was later destroyed by Japan at Tsushima, widening the discussion beyond Sweden and France. The closing argument moves from individual ship design to procurement action and reaction. A ship optimized for local defence could still influence what rival states chose to build.

evidence.note: The coastal-defence ships and their successors may have helped prompt Russian fleet expansion before much of that enlarged force was destroyed at Tsushima.

segments.summary: The video closes by linking these coastal-defence ships and their successors to the Russian naval expansion later destroyed at Tsushima.
